risks:
Human realism in the closest shots (the tableau, the slats, the dress, the locket look). Mitigations:
- Her face stays under wet hair, except one iris-less eye.
- Harlan's face is never rendered.
- In the locket look, the locket is sharp and she is soft in the depth of field, held 2.5 s or less.
- Backlight, lightning cuts, film grain and stop-motion throughout; every lit shot under 3 s.

Wet long hair from scratch can look plastic. Use clumped cards with wet specular, drip particles, a spring chain and a low-detail version beyond 6 m, and prototype it in M1 weeks 1-2 alongside the stop-motion A/B test.

The finale fights ten minutes of conditioning. Mitigations: the ledger and letter make the logic explicit; the locket rule works even mid-chase; the nonstop bell frames the moment; a prompt appears after the first failure; after two failures she waits.

Players who skip documents may miss the twist. Every document is 60 words or fewer, and the twist also reads without text: the wreck field, your plate on the can, the padlock outside the hatch, the sack, the knifed photos, HARLAN in the guest book.
The thunder and bell rules may go unnoticed. Each is demonstrated before it is needed (B02 bell, B06 thunder), the storm rhythm is regular, and there are assists and captions.
Bell decay could soft-lock B08. The 40 s floor resets on death, three thunder rolls fit in 40 s at the B08 storm cadence, and rumbles lengthen after failures.

Rope-rig readability underpins escape-theorem step 2. Use one mechanism everywhere: the pulley sound in B02, the rope visibly running in C2, the rope zip overhead in the finale, the bolt box clanking when you rattle the door.
The systemic locket rule adds a branch (finale before fuel). The ending then waits on the can in a quiet house; test this path explicitly in M2.

Browser performance. Keep one shadow caster in play; bake lightmaps (KTX2); use portal culling one floor at a time; instance the wrecks; pre-warm shaders; offer quality tiers with dynamic resolution. The lighting bake pipeline is the critical path and must exist in week 1.
Synthesized audio carries the AI's readability. Prototype drip, drip-stop, crack and gurgle in M1, keep the gurgle short and low, and use no synthesized voices.
AI fairness in a small house. Use the deterministic node graph and room-graph hearing, tune radii per room, never relocate her in view, guarantee the loops, cap hide checks, and add post-death grace.
The procedural handwriting font blocks every readable. Budget it in M2 week 1.

Scope cap: 9 spaces plus the car set. If M2 slips, turn the pump and mailbox into silhouettes, cut the wrecks to 3 variants plus fog cards, re-grade the sting car instead of re-trimming it, and cut the look-up pose.
Moral weight: the player sends a man to his death. His crimes frame it (guest book, cars, your plate, the padlock), and the sting makes the cost register.
Photosensitivity and content: flashes never exceed 3 Hz; ship a reduced-flash mode and a content warning (domestic violence, murder, drowning).
Browser input: the first click is 'turn the ignition key', which unlocks audio and pointer lock; pause whenever pointer lock is lost; QA on Chrome, Edge, Firefox and Safari.

Length: 12.5 min planned, with a first-time median of 13-14 min. Cutscenes run about 3.5 min, about 1 min of it interactive, and can be skipped on replay. If playtests run over 15 min, trim C1 and the bell floor first.
M3 polish debt concentrates in Ada's LOOK and stutter, the tell sounds, lightning and baked light, and per-room AI tuning. Protect that time over any new content.

scores.title: THE KEEPING
scores.notes: Strongest horror craft and client fidelity. The twist gives every fixed beat a second meaning: the bell is wired to the parlor as his signal, the door runs on his rope, he stops the second stroke on purpose, and 'both look at you' happens because he turns her face so she sees yours. The escape is a real deduction from one motif, faces (the sack, crepe over mirrors, knifed photos, her head-lift to inspect faces). It climaxes by reversing the rules the player has learned: stand still, light on, let her look. Clearest chaser language of the three: constant drip, drip stops = listening, bone crack = she can see, gurgle within 5 m, drying footprints, candles leaning toward her. The storm is a system too (thunder masks noise), and it drives the best mid-game set piece: prying the boards inside the thunder while the sack-man watches from the foot of the stairs in a flash. Other highlights: He Looks Up (your car pushed in among nine dead cars), your plate chalked on an empty can, the dress scene for emotional weight, and a sting that restages 'both of them look at you' with Harlan's head in a sack. Escape-clarity score counts deduction satisfaction. Weaknesses: heaviest scope (10 spaces at the cap, plus a pickup dash, the 9-car field, a dawn walk that exposes assets, cloth interactions, six Harlan animation sets). About 4 minutes of cutscene in 13.5 risks a first play running long. Seams: the GAS sign blurs 'ask to stay the night'. The locked parlor door 'opens for her' with no cause. Ada pulls off a dust sheet the player already pulled. Harlan's nonstop bell in B10 needs framing so the bell rule doesn't read as broken.

scores.title: HEADLIGHTS
scores.notes: Best-produced and most photoreal-aware. 8 spaces, only the front facade built, the car model reused as the wreck, every asset tagged M1/M2/M3, lightmap and handwriting-font risks called out, and the whole game stays at night. The flashlight drowning in the bath and the switch to a carried oil lamp is the best act change in any of the three designs: new light, new mood, new lure mechanic. Standout set pieces: hiding underwater while her hair drifts over your face; winding a loud clock under threat; the chime stopping her mid-lunge so she brushes past you. The 3 o'clock motif and the shop bells on every door are cohesive, readable tells, and 'lightning never reveals you' is a clean tuning rule. The ROOMS/VACANCY sign plus a one-line thought make client beat 1 airtight. Lower scores on this lens: Ray's note dictates the solution almost word for word and a card lists the rules, so it is the clearest escape but the least deduced. The twist's key rule ('whoever takes her head, she follows') sits on an optional drawer page, a fairness risk. The back-seat mirror sting is a familiar trope (BEHELD uses it too). The man refuelling your car offscreen removes a player goal. Small seam: the doorbell lure sends her downstairs, but the splash comes from the upstairs bath.

scores.title: BEHELD
scores.notes: Most rigorous systems spec: states in priority order, hearing computed on the room graph, a testable hide rule, board-then-room bell answering with predictable timing windows, a chatelaine jingle whose rhythm tracks her speed, and 8-12 fps stop-motion movement that hides animation flaws. Also post-reload grace and escalation. Good set pieces: lifting the key ring off its hook two paces behind her kneeling body; her head flopping upside down as she checks under a bed; the man's headlights sweeping through your wardrobe slats as he abandons you; performing the keeping through the narrowed sack view as she lays her own neck on the block. Weakest fiction: 1989 + 37 years puts the game in 2026, and phones are never addressed. The '91 note says 'KEEP HER, THEN GO', yet its writer stayed 37 years. A scripted outside-to-inside relocation (the bulkhead scare) undercuts rule readability. The finale follows a recipe from the ledger ('Bell, sack, dark, block, knife, box') rather than a deduction. The burlap man leaves around minute five, so the figure is lost as a recurring dread presence. The cellar and parlor-cellar-parlor-cellar backtracking add space and time. Many small systems (bottles, cupped beam, shared breath/sprint meter) thin out the polish of a 13-minute game. The back-seat sting is well-worn. It contributes systems, not story.

graft_list: (HEADLIGHTS) Firm up client beat 1: hang a hand-painted 'ROOMS / VACANCY' board under Harlan's lantern-lit GAS sign, and add one subtitle-only thought at the car: 'Nothing for 48 miles. They'll have to let me stay the night.' The lure now baits lodgers, which fits his trap.

(HEADLIGHTS) Production discipline: tag every space, prop, animation and sound M1/M2/M3; freeze layout and script at M2. M1 exit test: first-time strangers can state 'drip = near, drip stops = listening, crack/hand to head = she sees' after one play, at 60 fps on an integrated GPU.
(HEADLIGHTS) Build only the front facade and porch in detail; the sides and back dissolve into fog and rain. Reuse the player sedan for every field wreck and for the sting traveler's car.

(HEADLIGHTS) Lighting pipeline first: Blender-Python auto-UV2, lightmap bake and export in week 1. Bake a normal-night and a lightning variant per room and blend them on each flash (instead of a global exposure pulse). Pre-warm shaders before the first flash and the first chase.
(HEADLIGHTS) Stage Harlan's non-interactive appearances (pushing your car, standing at the foot of the stairs) as 2-3 static poses revealed by successive lightning flashes, not continuous animation.
(HEADLIGHTS) Budget a procedural single-stroke handwriting font with ink wobble for the diary, letter, guest book, chalked plates and the wet 'HARLAN'.
(HEADLIGHTS) Cross-floor drip tell: water beads and drips from the ceiling where she stands on the floor above. Useful in the kitchen (B10) and hall (B11).
(HEADLIGHTS) Accessibility: optional captions/icons for her tells (drip stops, crack, gurgle, bell) and a reduced-flash mode with ~150 ms flash fade-in.

(HEADLIGHTS, tuning choice) Lightning does not count as 'lit' for her sight, so the storm is purely the player's ally (thunder cover) and the flash stays a scare and vista device. Her sight is already gated behind the telegraphed LOOK, so this is tuning, not a fairness fix.
(BEHELD) Stop-motion quantization: sample Ada's pose at 8-12 fps with random held or dropped frames, keeping root motion at full rate. Cheap, distinctive, and it hides animation flaws.
(BEHELD) Her head flops upside down into view when she bends to check a low hide (the under-stair closet, under Harlan's iron bed). Cheap with the existing spring-joint neck, and a signature image.

(BEHELD) AI implementation: an authored node graph with scripted door and stair traversal instead of a navmesh. Hearing attenuates on the room graph (walls/floors counted, open-stairwell exception) instead of raycasts. Explicit state priority order. Testable hide rule: safe unless she had line of sight on entry within the last 2 s, or you are audible within 2 m.
(BEHELD) After a death she restarts at the anchor farthest from the player, PATROL-only with hearing -30% for 20 s.
(BEHELD) Escalation tied to story turns: once her door is pried, and again after she finds the cut hem, shorten her listen-stops and raise her LOOK frequency.
(BEHELD) Post-sprint panting audible (~2-3 m) for a few seconds, even inside a hide, with no meter UI. Teaches 'break line of sight early'.
cut_list: Bathroom (U2) as a playable room: make it a closed door with tub-slosh audio and light under the door. Keep it as her patrol anchor so B05's exit beat survives, and move the sack/twine/scissors mask kit to Harlan's bedroom. This cuts one space and removes an optional detour into her nest.
Separate pickup-dashboard set for the sting: use a re-trimmed sedan interior (different colour, blinking fuel lamp).

Daylight/sunrise walk through the dead-car field in B12: switch to blue-hour mist, 30-40 s. Your car sits at the NEAR end of the row (he pushed it last, so this costs nothing narratively). The nine wrecks stay a lightning-only vista, never lit by day.
Harlan's continuous car-push animation: replace with lightning-flash static poses.
Ada's dust-sheet pull in B09: it contradicts the player's own sheet pull and costs a cloth interaction. She finds the dress already exposed and her hand goes to the cut hem.
The unexplained 'parlor door opens for her' in B11: Harlan unbolts it himself, cleaver raised (his nightly reflex), which also stages the shadow-play.
The immediate 'raise the locket' prompt: surface it only after the first failed approach. The restart-with-locket-raised assist already covers stuck players, and this keeps the deduction payoff.

The ambiguity in Harlan's nonstop B10 bell: frame it as the same rule turned against you. All night the bell pulled her down to the parlor while you were upstairs; now you are on the parlor's floor. Make it audible as the drip coming down the main stair toward you.
The jerry can held in hand through the finale: stow it as inventory (no hand model) so the finale's hands are flashlight + locket only.

Readable 1976 calendar and the $40: redundant with the letter and bus ticket. Keep readables to the guest book, three diary pages and the letter, each 60 words or fewer, to protect the 10-15 min budget.
Harlan's frantic bell-ringing glimpse: audio only.
DO NOT IMPORT (HEADLIGHTS/BEHELD): the back-seat rear-view-mirror sting. It is a familiar trope and weaker than the mirrored parlor tableau.
DO NOT IMPORT (HEADLIGHTS/BEHELD): a player-performed beheading. It breaks this story's arc (Ada ends Harlan) and pushes gore toward the player.
DO NOT IMPORT (BEHELD): throwable bottles, the chatelaine jingle (duplicates the drip), the cupped beam and the breath/stamina meter UI. Too many systems for a 13-minute game.
DO NOT IMPORT (HEADLIGHTS/BEHELD): a rules card or note that spells out the solution. It kills the deduction.
DO NOT IMPORT (BEHELD/HEADLIGHTS): a cellar, or the man refuelling your car offscreen. The kitchen can-row with your chalked plate is the better clue and payoff.
judgements.rationale:
Overall is weighted by this judge's lens (dread, fairness, chaser readability, deduction satisfaction, memorable set pieces and ending, fidelity to the client beats). It is not a mean. On raw criterion averages HEADLIGHTS edges THE KEEPING (about 8.5 vs 8.3) because it wins buildability, running time and photoreal payoff. Those are production strengths, and they graft cleanly: facade-only exterior, M1/M2/M3 tagging, normal and lightning lightmap variants, flash poses, a procedural handwriting font.

THE KEEPING's advantages are structural and cannot be retrofitted onto another story. (a) Its twist gives every fixed client beat a second meaning: the bell wired to the parlor is his signal, the door runs on his rope, the second stroke is stopped on purpose, and both look at you because he turns her face to yours. (b) The escape is actually deduced from one motif, faces (sack, crepe-covered mirrors, knifed photos, her head-lift), and the climax reverses the rules the player spent ten minutes learning: stand still, light on, let her look. (c) Its sting restages the client's own 'both of them look at you' with Harlan's head in a sack, the most memorable single ending on offer. It also has the most readable threat language (drip, drip stops, crack, gurgle, thunder cover, bell lure) and real emotional weight in the dress scene.

HEADLIGHTS' shortfalls are at the story level and don't graft away: Ray's note dictates the solution, the twist's key rule sits on an optional page, and the back-seat sting is a trope that BEHELD shares. BEHELD has the best systems spec but the loosest fiction: an implied 2026 setting with no answer to phones, 'KEEP HER, THEN GO' written by a man who stayed 37 years, a scripted outside-to-inside relocation, and a recipe finale. It contributes AI implementation and animation tricks, not story.

THE KEEPING's own problems are scope at the 10-space cap, a dawn walk that exposes assets, and a handful of seams: the GAS sign vs. 'ask to stay the night', the parlor door 'opening for her', the double dust-sheet pull, the framing of the B10 bell, and the immediate locket prompt. The cut list and HEADLIGHTS' production discipline fix all of them. That brings it to about 9 spaces, all at night or blue hour, with the ~13-minute single route and the single ending intact.

scores.title: THE KEEPING
scores.notes:
FIDELITY 8: Beats 1-4 are intact and cleverly recontextualised: the rope opens the door, and he turns her face by the hair so both of them look. But the car dies under a lantern-lit GAS sign, so the house promises fuel and 'ask to stay the night' gets muddied.
HORROR 9: The strongest of the three: the GAS sign as bait, nine dead cars in lightning, your own plate chalked on an empty can, the cistern hatch padlocked from outside, prying boards inside the thunder, the drip-stop and bone-crack tells, the 'stand still and let her look' inversion, and the mirrored sting.
CLARITY 8: An elegant, deducible chain grounded in the diary, the letter and objects in the house. But it is the longest chain of the three and ends in a counterintuitive stand-still action that needs a contextual prompt.
BUILDABILITY 5 (heaviest):
- 10 spaces (the brief's cap) plus sedan and pickup interiors, nine field cars and a dawn exterior walk.
- Hero one-offs: treadle machine, dress dummy with a cuttable wedding dress, hinged locket, 1950s pump, lantern sign, bell-wire runs, rope-and-pulley rig, 12 chalked cans.
- Six animated Harlan appearances, including pushing a car, rocking, bell-ringing and a fall.
- Two Ada hand-contact beats: the dust sheet and hem, and taking the locket from the player.
- About 4.2 min of cutscenes, roughly 30% of runtime.
PHOTOREAL 7: The strengths are excellent: the shadow-play beheading, a Harlan whose face is never rendered, a lightning vista of low-detail cars, and the cheapest lighting plan of the three (one shadowed spot, lightning as an exposure pulse). Against that:
- A dawn exterior with weeds and cars in flat light.
- A locket photo that must show a man's face in the beam.
- A 4-second look at arm's length under a hard flashlight, which would be the most exposed character shot of any design once the base is re-staged.
FIT 7: 13.4 min planned, but prying three boards on thunder timing, 75 s bell windows, about 6 documents and 4 min of cutscenes push a first playthrough to about 15-17 min.
M1 SLICE: It front-loads hero props before any gameplay exists: GAS sign with lantern box, 1950s pump, porch swing, rope rig, a tally wall of about 6,000 marks, rocking chair, sawbuck table, parlor spring bell, and the bathroom tub needed for the B05 exit. It also needs Harlan's hair-grip contact animation.

scores.title: BEHELD
scores.notes:
FIDELITY 7: Beat 1 leaves out the 'no choice but to ask to stay the night' moment. The car dies and you take the flashlight from the glovebox; shelter appears only as a B02 goal. The Keeper's pickup parked in the yard also weakens 'no other choice'.
HORROR 7: The tension is systemic (the vigil on the landing, lifting the keys two paces behind her, the pitch-black cellar), but there are few set pieces. The bulkhead scare ('outside, then inside seconds later') breaks the design's own no-teleport rule. The back-seat knock sting is a familiar trope.
CLARITY 7: The ledger spells out the ritual ('Bell, sack, dark, block, knife, box'). But the finale has five simultaneous fail conditions (bell, light, noise, standing on the mark, wearing the sack), which invites trial and error. The bulkhead barred with 'She's out there' is an imposed gate.
BUILDABILITY 6: The man is nearly free: one opening performance, then only headlights. Against that:
- A cellar, a bulkhead on a second face of the house, a 90 m road strip and a 60 m climb.
- AI across three levels and two stairs.
- Systems sprawl with a long tuning tail: throwable bottles with physics, a shared breath/sprint meter, a cupped beam, the 5-bell ANSWER routine, key theft, can filling, boxing the head.
PHOTOREAL 6: It has the two best masking tricks of the three (8-12 fps stop-motion animation, the sack view in the finale). But the rooms are generic with no signature vista. Three shadow casters, one of them a fire point light with cube shadows, plus standing-water reflections tax an M1 at Medium. There is a dawn drive, and the under-bed check with her head upside down exposes the face.
FIT 6: 13.75 min planned, but variance is high: ritual retries, bottle and vigil timing, an 8 s can fill and a long exterior walk. A first playthrough likely runs 16-20 min.
M1 SLICE: The 90 m road, the 60 m drive, the pickup and its headlight sweep, the parlor with block, knife, box and fire, the Blue Room and the under-bed head flop. The ANSWER routine (bell board first, then the room) must already work in M1 because B05 teaches it.

scores.title: HEADLIGHTS
scores.notes:
FIDELITY 9: The most faithful beat 1: HARROW HOUSE - ROOMS, a VACANCY plate, and the subtitle 'They'll have to let me stay the night.' Then the door opens on the first chime, the player freezes, both look, and she chases you upstairs. The clue that she stopped the clock is planted inside the fixed chase.
HORROR 8: The chime-counted opening, hiding underwater beneath her drifting hair, the flashlight dying and leaving you an oil lamp, 12 loud crank clicks under threat, the compelled walk past you, and a sting built from the tells the player has learned. The back-seat reveal is a familiar trope.
CLARITY 9: One linear chain: bell cord, bath, crank, clock, chime, stroke, door. It is clued by objects (the ticking dies as she passes, hands at 3:01, weights down, the splash, footprints) and by the Rules card on the wall.
BUILDABILITY 8 (lightest):
- 8 spaces plus one car set, only two ground-floor rooms, and only the front wall of the house.
- The wreck under the tarp reuses the car model, and both characters share one skeleton.
- Night only, with no dawn lighting pass.
- Fuel is handled off-screen, so there is no carry-can, clank or pour system.
- Every asset is tagged M1/M2/M3 against measurable gates.
- Costs: the clock mechanics, the tub water and underwater view, the carried-lamp system, five hide types, and a 2x2 set of lighting bakes (Act 2/Act 3, each in a normal and a lightning version).
PHOTOREAL 9: The best weak-point hiding of the three: a man backlit by fire in a fixed composition, the stroke hidden in a lightning white-out, only her feet visible from under the bed, her silhouette through black water, her shadow past the nailed boards, a half-second mirror. The switch from cold flashlight to warm oil lamp is a built-in showcase. Two flaws:
- She lies face-up with her head hanging off the table, so gravity pulls the hair off her face at the threshold and again, under 1 m away, under the lamp in the finale.
- The lamp's all-direction cube shadows and the doubled bakes are the main costs at M1 Medium.
FIT 8: 13 min and 11 beats, with checkpoints that keep the wound weights. But the bath (2.25 min) and clock (2 min) beats run under threat, and with the card, four journal pages and the note, a first playthrough could stretch to 14-16 min.
DESIGN GAPS:
- Setting the lamp down in the parlor doorway parks her about 4 m from the clock, well inside the 12 m radius of the crank clicks.
- There is no ground-floor loop to break line of sight: the dining, kitchen and parlor rear doors are all barred.
M1 SLICE: Bounded: the car set, front wall and porch, the hall with the clock, the parlor with the fire, the stair, half the upper hall, the guest room and wardrobe.

graft_list: [THE KEEPING] Thunder masking. She cannot hear the player during the ~2.5 s thunder roll that starts ~1.5 s after each lightning flash. Show it once: thunder audibly swallows her footsteps outside the Keeper's room. Then B08 winding becomes a rhythm: flash, count, rumble, crank. This fixes the base's lamp-lure conflict (a lamp set in the parlor doorway parks her ~4 m from the clock, inside the 12 m click radius). Keep the storm rhythm regular, and flash more often after 2 deaths. No new assets; it reuses the lightning system.

[THE KEEPING] The drip stopping means she is listening. On any noise she freezes ~1 s with her head tilted and the drip pauses. The drip rate also tracks her speed (BEHELD's key-ring jingle idea applied to the existing drip). No new sounds.
[THE KEEPING] Candle flames lean toward her instead of only flickering, which gives a direction tell. One parameter on the existing candle-flame shader.

[THE KEEPING] Pre-written guestbook line. On entry, the newest line already shows tonight's date and 'in 3:00 a.m.' in wet ink with the name blank (an optional read at the lectern before the threshold). It pays off at checkout as 'S. Hale - in 3:00 a.m.'. Costs one extra paper texture.
[THE KEEPING] In-world assist. After 3+ deaths in one beat, a door's shop bell jingles at the far end of the floor and draws her away. Reuses the existing door-bell tell.
[THE KEEPING] The death cutaway ends in a bubbling drowning rush, tying every death to her 3 a.m. drowning in the bath. One synthesized sound.

[THE KEEPING] On the Medium preset, lightning is a global exposure and light-probe pulse. Keep blended night/lightning lightmaps only for the three rooms with windows (guest room, the upper hall's west window, the stair landing), at High.

[THE KEEPING] Production caps:
- Every document is 60 words or fewer with one key line (trim the four journal pages to fit).
- Every lit character shot is held under 3 s.
- Prototype the tell sounds (drip, drip stopping, neck creak, door bells, clock tick and chime) in M1, before art polish.

[BEHELD] Stop-motion animation. Drive Ada's pose at 8-12 fps with random held and skipped frames, while the camera and the world render at full rate, so flaws in the procedural animation read as intentional. In M1 week 1, prototype two options: quantize only the skeleton, or the whole pose including hair and cloth. The base runs hair and cloth as simple physics, and a rate mismatch could look broken rather than uncanny.

[BEHELD] Hearing through a hand-built room map. Weaken each noise by counting the doors, walls and floors between rooms on a hand-authored room graph, with no raycasts. Move her on a hand-authored path graph with scripted door and stair traversal instead of a navmesh. Deterministic, testable and cheap on an M1.

[BEHELD] Hood view for the final stroke. As part of 'hold to raise', the player pulls on a Keeper's hood hanging on the parlor mantel hook beside where the cleaver fell. It is automatic, so it can't be failed. An eyehole vignette and muffled audio hide the only shot of her head from under 1 m, and make 'you are the Keeper now' physical (lore: every Keeper since Silas wore one). The sting clue survives: the player pulls the hood off in the parlor after the stroke, yet a hood is lying on the passenger seat anyway.

[BEHELD] Grace period after reload. She restarts at the patrol point farthest from the player, out of sight, with reduced hearing for 20 s. Key items can't be lost, and a lamp that was set down returns to hand on reload, so the player can't soft-lock.

[BEHELD + THE KEEPING] Guaranteed loop for breaking line of sight. In Act 3 only, unbar the parlor's rear door (Ray's exit route) and the hall's rear door, joined by a short unlit service passage built from the modular kit. The clock beat then gets a hall, parlor and passage circuit. Total spaces become 9, and the fixed parlor camera composition is untouched.

[HEADLIGHTS self-fix] Move the drawer-page line ('Drove to the county line in '81. She was in the back seat. Whoever takes her head, she follows.') onto the back of Ray's fresh note. That puts the twist clue on the required path at no cost, as the base's own risk list already proposes.
cut_list: [HEADLIGHTS] Cut the face-up pose with her head hanging off the table, in both the opening and the finale. Lying on her back with her hair 'pooled on the floor', gravity strips the hair off an upside-down face at the threshold, and again under 1 m away under the lamp. Re-stage her face-down or on her side, head hanging forward, so the wet hair falls over her face like a curtain. For the 'both look' beat she lifts her head by the hair, which teaches the look tell in the very first scene.
[HEADLIGHTS] Cut the separate Act 2 and Act 3 bake for every room. The light the player carries is dynamic, so re-bake only the hall and the parlor (fire burning down to embers).
[HEADLIGHTS] Cut the per-room lightning lightmap versions, except in the three rooms with windows at High. Use the exposure/probe pulse everywhere else and on Medium.

[HEADLIGHTS] Cut cube shadows on the carried oil lamp. With the light at the camera, its shadows mostly fall behind the objects that cast them, out of view. Turn shadows on (512 cube map, updated ~30 times a second) only when the lamp is set down, where they read, for example her shadow thrown across the hall as she comes to the lure.
[HEADLIGHTS] Cut the gargled chase shriek; it is the synthesized voice most likely to sound electronic. Carry the chase with wet footfalls, the throat rattle and the string sting.

[HEADLIGHTS] Cut Ray's lit walk cycle and shorten the 400 m looping fog drive to about 40 s. Ray becomes a still figure with his back turned, stepping onto the verge in the headlights (one pose blend).

[HEADLIGHTS] Build every beat seen only by lightning (her hand at the clock, Ray at your car, the oak) as held poses or static silhouettes between flashes. No continuous animation and no simulated branch sway.

[HEADLIGHTS, conditional] Cut the under-bed hide only if M2 slips. It is the cheapest close encounter, and it can't show a face because only her feet are visible. The wardrobe, linen cupboard and under-stair closet are one slatted-cabinet family, and the tub is a set piece.

[HEADLIGHTS, keep] Don't add a puzzle to fetch fuel. Ray refueling off-screen saves building a can-carrying action, its clank noise and a pouring mechanic, and the empty can and open fuel cap tell the story.

[Don't import from THE KEEPING] The dawn walk through the field of cars, the pickup-dashboard set for the sting, the locket with a man's face photo, the treadle machine and cuttable wedding dress, Harlan's car-push and rocking-chair animations, and a 10-space map.

[Don't import from BEHELD] The cellar and bulkhead doors, throwable bottles with physics, the shared breath/sprint meter, the cupped beam, the 5-bell answering routine, stealing the key ring, filling the can, handling the head into the box, the under-bed check with her head upside down, and three shadow-casting lights.
judgements.rationale:
Judged on buildability and photoreal payoff, HEADLIGHTS is the best base.

**Scope:** It is the only design that sits well under the space cap: 8 spaces plus one car set, two ground-floor rooms, and only the front wall of the house. The tarped wreck reuses the car model, both characters share one skeleton, and it is night only, so there is no dawn lighting pass. It tags every asset M1/M2/M3 against measurable gates and has the most bounded M1 slice.

**Hiding the weak points:** It stages nearly every character beat to hide the weak links. The man is a backlit silhouette, the stroke happens inside a lightning white-out, the bed hide shows only her feet, and she is also seen through black water, as a shadow through boards, and in a half-second mirror flash.

**Payoff:** The flashlight dying and leaving an oil lamp is a built-in photoreal showcase that also becomes a mechanic. The 3 a.m. clock ties the bell, chime, door and ritual into the most deducible chain of the three, and beat 1 is the most faithful.

**THE KEEPING:** It is the better story and the scariest design, but it is the heaviest build: 10 spaces plus two vehicle interiors, nine field cars, a dawn exterior, hero props, a locket that needs a face, six animated Harlan appearances and about 4 min of cutscenes. Its M1 slice front-loads that art before any gameplay exists. Take its cheap systemic ideas (thunder masking, drip-stop, leaning flames, the pre-written guestbook line) and leave its content.

**BEHELD:** Its AI engineering and masking tricks are worth taking (stop-motion animation, hearing on a room map, the hood view). But the cellar, the systems sprawl, three shadow casters, generic rooms and high variance in playtime make it the riskiest route to a polished 10-15 minute game.

**Required fixes to the base:**
- Re-stage the face-up hanging head, since gravity uncovers the face.
- Add thunder masking so the 12-click clock still works with the lamp lure.
- Add an Act 3 ground-floor loop for breaking line of sight.
- Use the hood view for the final stroke.
- Move the twist line onto Ray's required note.
- Trim the lighting bakes and the lamp shadows to hold 60 fps on an M1 at Medium.

designs.title: THE KEEPING
designs.logline: Out of gas on an empty county road at night, you ring the bell of the only lit house for miles. Inside you walk in on a man in a feed-sack mask beheading a woman, and she turns her head to look at you. She hunts you through the house until you work out whose face she has really been looking for.
designs.lore:
THE HOUSE. Stroud's Gas & Feed served County Road 9 until its one pump ran dry in the early seventies. Harlan Stroud inherited it from his father. In 1968 he married Ada Lind, a seamstress from Carvel, twenty miles east. By 1976 the marriage was locks and bruises. Ada saved sewing money in a biscuit tin, wrote to her sister Ruth, and bought a seat on the 6:10 bus for Tuesday 12 October. Harlan found the tin. On the night of the 11th he did what he had always threatened: he held her under in the rain cistern beneath the kitchen floor and padlocked the hatch. He told Carvel she had run off with a feed salesman. Nobody looked for her, nobody mourned her and nobody buried her.

WHAT SHE IS. Whatever the water keeps comes back up. Three nights later Ada climbed out. She is a revenant, one of the unmourned drowned, and she wants exactly one thing: the face of the man who held her under. The cistern clouded her eyes, so she has to lift her head close to a face to know it. Any face that is not his, she drags down into the water with her, and each stranger buys weeks of quiet. She is not mindless. She remembers her room, her dress and the bell. And she learns.

WHAT HE IS. Nothing supernatural. He is a man who murdered his wife, made himself her jailer and then her farmer. His mother's receipt book said: take the head and give it back to the water. That holds her for one night. He has done it about six thousand times and marked each one with a pencil tally on the parlor wall. He hides from her the only way that works: a feed sack over his head, black crepe over every mirror, and his face scratched out of every photograph. The one image he could not destroy, the locket, he believes went down the well with her. In 1977 a drifter kept her quiet for a month, and Harlan learned he could buy rest. He repainted the GAS sign and lights its lantern with fuel siphoned from the last guest's car. He wired the doorbell and every bell pull to ring in the parlor, hung the front door on a rope, nailed the windows and kept a guest book: eleven names, nine cars in the east field. It has to be her who takes them; when he killed one himself, it did not hold her for an hour. He tells his diary he does it 'so she can't walk the road'. That part is also true.

THE TWIST (the opening recontextualised). Nothing in the opening was chance. The sign that promised fuel was bait, lit with a dead man's gasoline. The bell you rang was his signal. The door that 'opened by itself' was his rope. The beheading you walked in on was his nightly chore, and he stopped the second stroke on purpose. 'Both of them looked at you' because he took her by the hair and turned her face to the doorway so she would see yours. Then he let the rope go, and the slam and the stairs herded you upward like the eleven before you. He is not a killer caught in the act, and he is not the tragic keeper his diary pretends to be. He is her murderer, and you are the meal. She was never hunting you. She is hunting him, and she can't see him.

THE WAY OUT. The last image of Harlan's face is in the locket he gave her. The night before she died, Ada sewed it into the hem of her wedding dress, beside her bus ticket. Hold his face up in your light and let her look.

THE STING. She learns. Whoever holds the rope keeps the house.

characters.name: The Traveler
characters.role: Player character: first person, silent, unnamed. Driving through in October 1994, so there is no phone, only a cassette deck and a fuel needle below E.
characters.appearance: Never seen. Only leather driving gloves, a rain-dark coat sleeve and a steel two-cell flashlight. Drives a tired late-80s sedan with plate RVX-318, which is shown clearly in the opening and matters later.
characters.behavior: No speech and no monologue. Emotion is carried by the camera and the hands: the lock-up at the threshold, a trembling beam when Ada is near, strained breathing in hides, the heartbeat. The only intent is to survive the night and then leave.

characters.name: Ada Stroud (the woman)
characters.role: The single AI chaser. A revenant, one of the unmourned drowned, and the story's true victim.
characters.appearance: Slight and barefoot, in a sodden ivory cotton nightgown stained grey-green with cistern silt. Grey-blue skin shows only at the hands and feet. Very long black hair is plastered wet over her whole face; one clouded, milk-white eye is the most ever shown. Water drips from her constantly. Tonight her neck is half-severed, so the head hangs forward or lolls onto a shoulder (procedural spring joint) unless she lifts it with her hand. A pale line on her throat shows where a locket chain once sat.
characters.behavior: Jerky, stuttering motion with held frames and sudden stillness. While her head hangs she is blind and hunts by sound and by the warmth of light. To see, she must lift her head in her hand with an audible bone crack, which is the game's key tell. She opens ordinary doors, slowly. She always goes to a ringing bell. She inspects faces, because any face might be his. In private moments, such as with her wedding dress, she is heartbreakingly human. She learns.

characters.name: Harlan Stroud (the man)
characters.role: Scripted presence only, never an AI chaser. Husband, murderer, jailer and trapper.
characters.appearance: A big, stooped man in his sixties. A burlap feed sack over his head, with a faded 'STROUD FEED & SEED' stencil, eye holes cut unevenly, tied at the neck with twine. Flannel shirt, suspenders, heavy black rubber butcher's apron, rubber boots, work gloves and a hog cleaver. His face is never shown to the player, not even at his death, where the unmasking is only a shadow on the wall.
characters.behavior: Slow and patient. He never runs and never attacks you ('She has to take them herself'). He has five staged appearances: the opening; pushing your car into the field in the rain; looking up at your window; standing at the foot of the stairs in a lightning flash; and rocking in the parlor, seen through the floor grate, where he tilts the sack up at you. The creak of his rocking chair drifts up through the floors as a dread metronome and stops when he moves. When threatened, he rings the parlor bell to summon her.

characters.name: The next traveler
characters.role: Point of view for the final sting only.
characters.appearance: Unseen. Only a pickup-truck dashboard with a blinking fuel light.
characters.behavior: Knocks, rings the bell and freezes on the threshold, repeating the player's opening.

house_layout.name: County Road 9 & the GAS sign
house_layout.size_m: ≈12 × 40 playable: 7 m two-lane asphalt, gravel shoulders, flooded ditch; fog wall at ≈35 m
house_layout.description: The dead road. A hand-painted GAS sign on a post with a tin lantern box, lit with fuel siphoned from the last victim. A rusted STROUD mailbox, a fence line with reflector posts, and a flooded ditch. Your car dies here in the opening, you drive away from here at dawn, and the next traveler's pickup stops here in the sting. Mostly seen from the car, plus a short walk to the gate.
connections: EXT2: gravel drive to the north
key_contents: player's sedan, plate RVX-318 (until Harlan moves it)

house_layout.name: Yard, porch & east field
house_layout.size_m: drive ≈25 × 5; covered porch 9 × 2.5; east-field vista ≈60 × 30 with low-detail cars
house_layout.description: A gravel drive leads past a dead 1950s pump to a sagging porch. The swing creaks by itself and every window sash shows nail heads. To the right of the door, candlelight leaks through the parlor shutters. The front door has a knocker and a brass bell-pull knob whose wire runs inside to the parlor. East of the drive, nine dead cars sit in the weeds. They are a lightning vista from upstairs, and the player walks through them in the dawn ending.
connections: G1: front door (rope-bolted from the parlor)
key_contents: dead gas pump: price dial frozen at 1976, 'STROUD'S GAS & FEED'
front door: knocker, bell-pull knob, counterweight bolt
row of 9 dead cars (+ yours after B07)

house_layout.name: Entrance hall & main stair
house_layout.size_m: 3.6 × 9, ceiling 3.2; stair 1.1 wide, 16 risers rising north along the west wall
house_layout.description: Side-hall plan. The front door is at the south end, the stair rises along the left (west) wall, and the parlor door is on the right (east) just inside: the first room on the right. A hall table holds a candle and the open guest book. Black crepe covers a tall mirror. The wedding portrait has the groom knifed out. A rope on three pulleys runs along the east cornice from the door bolt into the parlor, next to the bell wires. At the north end are the shut back passage to the kitchen and an under-stair closet (hide). This is the stage for both the opening and the finale.
connections: G2: parlor door (locked after the opening)
G3: back passage (north end; locked from the kitchen side until B10)
key_contents: guest book (11 names ruled through; tonight's date written, name left blank)

house_layout.name: The parlor: the first room on the right
house_layout.description: Harlan's room, and the house's altar. A long sawbuck table under a rubber sheet with a zinc bucket. His rocking chair faces the door. The north wall is covered up to the picture rail in pencil tallies, about six thousand, one per night. The spring bell above the door is wired to the doorbell and to every bell pull in the house. The door rope is tied off at a cleat. A candle stands on the mantel under a crepe-covered mirror, and the hog cleaver is here. The player never walks around this room: it is seen from the threshold (opening, finale, sting) and from above through the bedroom's floor grate.
connections: U3: floor heat register above (view only)

house_layout.name: Kitchen, pantry & cistern hatch
house_layout.description: A cold iron stove and a pump sink. In the floor is the cistern hatch, padlocked on the outside, its edges splintered upward from beneath, with water seeping between the boards. The storm-swollen cistern sloshes below and once thumps against the lid. A 1976 calendar has Tuesday 12 circled '6:10'. A row of jerry cans is chalked with licence plates and full of the dead travelers' fuel, plus one fresh empty can chalked RVX-318. The back door is boarded and bricked. The back stair arrives in the north-east corner, and the passage leads west to the hall.
connections: G1: back passage to the hall

house_layout.name: Upper hallway & landing
house_layout.size_m: 2 × 9, ceiling 2.9; balustrade open to the stairwell
house_layout.description: The stair arrives at the north end, and the hallway runs back south along the balustrade, so you can see down into the hall. A runner rug down the middle is quiet; the bare-board margins are loud, and the worst creakers show visible gaps. The armoire (first hide) stands midway on the east wall. The south-end window is the main lightning source. There is a covered mirror and a knifed photo of the couple at the pump in 1970. Doors: bathroom (north, facing the stair top), Ada's room (east, north end, nailed with three boards), Harlan's bedroom (east, south end).

house_layout.name: Bathroom
house_layout.description: Ada's upstairs nest: she stands in the clawfoot tub of cold, pinkish water where Harlan soaks his rubber apron. Crepe covers the medicine-cabinet mirror. On a stool sit spare feed sacks, twine and scissors, his mask-making kit. An optional lore detour, and a risky one, because this is where she rests.

house_layout.name: Harlan's bedroom
house_layout.description: Directly above the parlor. An iron bed, and a nightstand with his farm-ledger diary and a kerosene lamp. The wardrobe (hide) is packed with strangers' coats, a handbag and a trucker cap. An embroidered bell pull hangs by the bed. The east window over the field is nailed shut, with the claw hammer and a coffee can of nails on the sill. The washstand mirror is under crepe. A snapshot shows Ada at her sewing machine beside the dress. A cast-iron floor heat register looks straight down into the parlor.
connections: G2: view through the floor grate
key_contents: snapshot of Ada and the dress

house_layout.name: Ada's sewing room
house_layout.description: Nailed shut and untouched since 1976. Dust sheets cover a chair, a trunk and a dress dummy. The treadle sewing machine stands at the window with her unsent letter trapped under the presser foot. A sewing basket holds shears. Her wedding dress is on the dummy, with the bundle sewn into its hem. There is a snapshot of Ada and Ruth. A heavy wardrobe (hide) stands against the north wall to hide the door to the servants' stair, and its back boards are loose.
connections: U5: through the back of the wardrobe
key_contents: wedding dress with hem bundle (locket, ticket, $40)

house_layout.name: Servants' back stair
house_layout.size_m: 0.8 wide, 14 steep risers with one winder, ≈1 × 3.5 footprint
house_layout.description: Enclosed, pitch black and curtained with 18 years of cobwebs, with a single tight turn. The cistern's slosh grows louder as you descend. It is the only way down that avoids the hall, and Ada never uses it.

beats.title: Empty
beats.description: Opening cutscene, in-engine. Night, hard rain and fog. Wipers, radio static between stations, the fuel needle under E and the low-fuel chime. A sign slides past: NEXT SERVICES 48 MI. Out of the dark comes a hand-painted GAS sign lit by a lantern in a tin box, and a STROUD mailbox. The engine coughs and dies, and the car rolls to a stop. Beyond the gate stands the house: peeling clapboard, nailed shutters, a dead pump, a porch swing moving on its own, and one window to the right of the door leaking candlelight. Lightning. The camera rises past the rear of the car, where the taillights glow on plate RVX-318, as you step into the rain. There is no other light for miles; the only choice is to ask to stay the night. Tension 2→4.
beats.player_goal: Watch; step out of the car.
beats.setpiece: The car dies under the lantern-lit GAS sign; lightning reveals the house.

beats.title: Stroud's
beats.description: First control, where the flashlight becomes essential. Walk up the gravel drive past the dead 1950s pump: nozzle dry, price dial frozen at 1976 prices, faded 'STROUD'S GAS & FEED'. The sign's lantern hisses behind you. On the porch the swing creaks and nail heads glint in every sash. Through the parlor shutters on the right, a shadow rises and falls in rhythm. Knock: nothing. Pull the bell: it rings inside, off to the right, and stops. A long beat. Then the latch clacks and the front door swings open by itself onto a dark hall. Tension 4→6.
beats.player_goal: Find someone who will let you stay: knock, then ring.
beats.setpiece: The door that opens by itself.

beats.title: The First Room on the Right
beats.description: Inside: a candle on the hall table beside the open guest book (optional read: eleven names ruled through, and tonight's date written with the name left blank). Black crepe covers the hall mirror. A wedding photograph has the groom's face scratched out. Anyone who looks up sees a rope on pulleys running along the cornice from the door into the parlor. A wet, rhythmic sound comes from the parlor door on the right, which is ajar. At the threshold the controls lock and the player freezes. Candlelight throws the scene onto the wall as shadow-play: a man in a feed-sack mask and rubber apron stands over a woman bent across a long table on a rubber sheet. Her neck has already been cut once; his second stroke is raised, and stops. He takes a fistful of her wet hair and turns her face to the doorway. Behind the hair, one clouded eye opens. The sack's eyeholes turn to you. Both of them look at you for three heartbeats. He lets the rope slip from its cleat, and behind you the front door slams and the bolt drops. She slides off the table and rises, head lolling on the half-cut neck. Tension 6→10.
beats.player_goal: Frozen at first, then run.
beats.setpiece: The beheading tableau in shadow; the double look; the door slam.

beats.title: Up
beats.description: Scripted chase with a guaranteed near-miss. The front door rattles uselessly, the kitchen passage at the far end of the hall is shut, and lightning shows the stair as the only way. She follows in stuttering bursts, one hand on the banister, head swinging. At the top, the hallway doubles back along the balustrade, so you can see her climbing below. A lightning flash through the end window picks out an armoire standing ajar. Dawdling means death, but a forgiving one. Tension 10.
beats.player_goal: Get away from her and hide.
beats.setpiece: Chase up the stairs, with her visible through the balusters.

beats.title: Hold Your Breath
beats.description: First hide, taught by demonstration. Through the slats you hear wet slaps on the stairs and the drip. At the top she stops, and the drip stops too: she is listening. She comes down the hall and stands at the slats. The wet gurgle, then a crack of bone as her hand lifts her head, and the hair parts on one milk-white eye in a lightning flash. Prompt: hold breath. She lowers her head, the drip resumes, and she turns into the bathroom with the slosh of stepping into the tub. Checkpoint. This ends the vertical slice. Tension 10→5.
beats.player_goal: Stay hidden and hold your breath while she looks.
beats.setpiece: The eye at the slats.

beats.title: His Room
beats.description: Stealth tutorial on a readable loop. She drifts between the tub, the stair top and the hallway; her wet footprints glisten and dry; the drip gives her away through walls. A thunderclap audibly swallows her footsteps, showing the masking rule before it is needed. Harlan's bedroom sits over the parlor. It holds his farm-ledger diary (the keeper's story, plus the lines that matter), a claw hammer and a coffee can of nails on the sill of a nailed window, an embroidered bell pull, and a wardrobe stuffed with strangers' coats (a hide among the eleven). A floor heat register looks straight down into the parlor: the tally-covered wall, the table, and the rocking chair, empty but still rocking. Optional detour: the bathroom stool of spare feed sacks, twine and scissors, where he makes his faces. Tension 5→6.
beats.player_goal: Look for a way out; read the diary; take the hammer.
beats.setpiece: The floor-grate view down into the parlor.

beats.title: He Looks Up
beats.description: Lightning floods the east field: nine dead cars in the weeds, rain drumming on their roofs. In the next flash, the man in the sack is pushing YOUR car (RVX-318) off the drive to join them. He stops and slowly lifts his head to your window. Darkness. In the next flash he is gone. Below, the front door opens and closes on its rope, and the rocking-chair creak resumes under your feet. The grate now shows him in the chair with the cleaver across his knees; if you peek, he tilts the sack up at you. Nobody is coming, and you are the next car. Tension 6→8→6.
beats.player_goal: Understand there is no help and no car.
beats.setpiece: The field of cars, and the man who looks up.

beats.title: Nailed Shut
beats.location: Upper hallway: Ada's door by the stair top
beats.description: The one door upstairs you can't open is nailed shut with three boards. Pull the bell in his room: far below, the parlor bell jangles and the drip recedes down the stairs. She has gone to the bell and scratches at the parlor door, which you can hear through the grate. Now pry, but every screech carries through the house, so pry inside the thunder: flash, count, rumble, pull. In one flash a figure stands at the foot of the stairs, sack tilted up, watching you through the balusters. In the next flash he is gone. If you pry outside the thunder she comes back up; hide in the armoire, and the boards you've already pried stay pried. Tension 5→8.
beats.player_goal: Open Ada's door without bringing her back.
beats.setpiece: Prying in the thunder; the watcher at the foot of the stairs.

beats.title: The Hem
beats.description: Untouched since 1976. Dust sheets cover everything, one of them over a dress dummy. A snapshot of Ada and her sister is pinned up. At the window, the treadle machine has an unsent letter trapped under the presser foot, ending mid-word. Cut the hem of the wedding dress with her shears to find a bundle: a 6:10 bus ticket for 12 October 1976, forty dollars, and a locket engraved 'A. from H. 1968'. Inside is a small water-stained photo of a young man, the only face of Harlan left in the world. The drip returns on the landing and comes through the door you opened. Hide in her wardrobe. Through the slats, she pulls the sheet off the dummy, finds her dress, finds the cut hem, and makes a long wet sound that is almost a sob. Her head lifts toward the wardrobe, and then she leaves. The wardrobe's back boards give way to cold air: the servants' stair he hid 18 years ago. Tension 6→9→4.
beats.player_goal: Find what Harlan fears; survive her visit.
beats.setpiece: Ada and her wedding dress, seen from the hide.

beats.title: What the Water Keeps
beats.description: A narrow stair choked with cobwebs, with one tight turn and the slosh below growing louder. In the kitchen, the cistern hatch in the floor is padlocked on the OUTSIDE, its edges splintered upward from beneath. The rain-swollen water sloshes under the boards, and something floating thumps once against the lid from below. A 1976 calendar has Tuesday 12 circled '6:10'. A row of jerry cans is chalked with licence plates and full of the dead travelers' siphoned fuel. At the end of the row sits a fresh, empty can already chalked RVX-318. Take a full one. Then the parlor bell starts ringing and doesn't stop: he has heard you, and he is calling her down. Tension 6→8.
beats.player_goal: Learn the truth; take fuel.
beats.setpiece: The thump from under the hatch; your plate on the empty can.

beats.title: Let Her Look
beats.location: Entrance hall: foot of the stair to the parlor threshold
beats.description: Lightning: she comes down the main stair toward the bell, head swinging, and turns to you. The front door is still bolted by the rope. Everything the night has taught you says run. Instead, raise the open locket into your flashlight beam and hold still. She comes close. The crack; her hand lifts her head; one eye, and the face in the locket. The bell stops dead. Her fingers close over the locket. She turns to the parlor door, and it opens for her. The camera holds the same threshold view as the opening. He stands with the cleaver raised; she walks into it; the candle dies. Lightning: on the wall, her shadow pulls the sack from his head. Next flash: her shadow lifts his cleaver. Black. One stroke, the bell once, then the long zip of the rope through its pulleys. Behind you, the front door swings open by itself onto grey dawn, and the parlor door closes by itself. Tension 8→10→2.
beats.player_goal: Show her his face.
beats.setpiece: The unmasking in shadow; the door opens for you.

beats.title: Dawn
beats.description: Release. Birdsong, dripping eaves, mist lying in the field. Walk out between the dead cars to your own at the end of the row. Pour the can (hold) and turn the key: two coughs, then the engine catches and the radio comes back mid-song. Roll down the drive past the pump; the GAS sign's lantern gutters out as you pass. In the mirror, the house sinks into the mist. Tension 2→1.
beats.player_goal: Leave.
beats.setpiece: The engine catches.

beats.title: The Keeping
beats.location: County Road 9 → hall → parlor threshold (another traveler)
beats.description: The final sting cutscene mirrors the opening shot. Weeks later, in the rain, a different dashboard. The lantern in the GAS sign is lit again. A knock, the bell, and the door opens by itself. The newest line in the guest book reads HARLAN in wet, clumsy capitals, ruled through, with tonight's date and a blank beneath it. In the first room on the right, Ada sits in his rocking chair with a round, heavy feed sack tied at the neck in her lap. The rocking stops. She lifts her own head in one hand, and with the other she lifts the sack by its knot and turns its eyeholes to the doorway, as he once turned hers. Both of them look at you. Smash to black, one bell, then the title. Tension 1→10→black.
beats.player_goal: None. Watch.
beats.setpiece: The mirrored tableau.

states: SCRIPTED: cutscenes and set pieces: the opening rise, the first chase (guaranteed near-miss), her visit to the dress, the finale
PATROL: slow stuttering walk (0.9 m/s) on the current floor's loop (upstairs: tub ↔ stair top ↔ hallway ↔ door thresholds); head hanging, so blind; drip audible
LISTEN: freezes about 1 s with her head tilted toward a noise; the drip stops
INVESTIGATE: walks (1.4 m/s) to the noise or light source, then LOOKs
LOOK: her hand lifts her head (1.2 s wind-up; 0.6 s if your beam touched her); sight is active for 3 s, then the head lowers
CHASE: jerky bursts at 3.2 m/s, head swinging; tracks you by quick sight glances and by the sound of you running
SEARCH: at the last known position, up to two LOOKs and nails dragged along plaster, then she stands at the nearest hide listening for 4–6 s
LURED: any bell pulls her out of PATROL, INVESTIGATE or SEARCH (never CHASE) to scratch at the parlor door for about 75 s, then she climbs back up
CATCH: grab and death cutaway
FINALE: ignores hides; approaches, stops at arm's length and LOOKs for a long 4 s if the locket is raised
chaser_ai.senses: SOUND (primary, always on). Every player action makes a noise with a radius: crouch-walk 1.5 m, walk 4 m, run 10 m, bare-board creaker 7 m, door slow/fast 3/8 m, prying 14 m, dropped item 8 m, gasp inside a hide 3 m. A closed door halves the radius. A floor between you cuts it by 60%, except through the open stairwell. She does not hear anything you do during a thunder roll: the 2.5 s rumble that follows each lightning flash by about 1.5 s. LIGHT (secondary). If your beam touches her body she does an instant fast LOOK. A beam sweeping within 6 m draws her to INVESTIGATE, because she feels light as warmth on her skin. Fixed candles and lamps don't lure her, but they light you up. SIGHT (conditional, the core rule). She sees only while her head is lifted: during LOOK, and in 1 s re-acquire glances during CHASE. Her cone is 60°, reaching 14 m if you are lit (beam on, lamplight or a lightning flash), 5 m if you are unlit in darkness, and 2 m if you are unlit and crouched. Being seen starts a CHASE. Being seen entering a hide means you are found.
chaser_ai.rules: 1) She never knows where you are without a sense event; no cheating. 2) Head down always means blind. 3) She LOOKs when she arrives where a noise came from, and at fixed look points (doorways, stair top). 4) She opens ordinary doors, slowly and audibly. She never opens the nailed door until it is pried, never the parlor door until the finale, and never uses the back stair. 5) Hides are slatted cabinets: the armoire, two wardrobes, the pantry and the under-stair closet. A hide is safe unless she saw you enter or you make noise inside. When she stands at your slats, hold your breath (about 6 s, with heartbeat and vignette); letting go early makes you gasp, and she opens the door. 6) To lose her, break line of sight and then stop running. After 4 s without sight or running noise she drops to SEARCH. 7) Bells override everything except CHASE. 8) Speeds. You: walk 1.6, run 3.6 (no stamina), crouch 0.9. Her: patrol 0.9, investigate 1.4, chase 3.2. Running in a straight line gains ground but never escapes her; corners and hides do. 9) There is only one of her, and she is never relocated where you could see it; scripted moves happen behind doors or floors. 10) Harlan never attacks ('She has to take them herself'). He is a scripted watcher, so the danger always reads as one body.
chaser_ai.tells: The drip is a constant, spatialized patter from her hair and gown, so you always know roughly where she is, even through walls. When the drip STOPS, she is listening: freeze. A bone crack and her hand rising to her jaw mean she is about to see (1.2 s warning): break line of sight or kill the light. Wet footprints glisten in the beam and dry out over about 60 s, showing where she has been and how recently. The wet gurgle from her half-cut throat means she is within about 5 m. Candle flames lean toward her and gutter as she passes. Nails dragging on plaster mean she is searching. Music: a low string cluster and heartbeat play during CHASE and drop to silence when she loses you. The parlor bell means she is going downstairs. Her head hanging means she is blind; her head held up in her hand means she can see.
chaser_ai.counterplay: Listen before you move. Walk on the runner and crouch on bare boards. Keep the flashlight off near her, and never put the beam on her body. When the drip stops, freeze. When you hear the crack, get out of her cone or into darkness. Break line of sight before you hide, and hold your breath when she is at the slats. Do anything loud (running, doors, prying) under the thunder. Pull a bell to send her down to the parlor door for about 75 s. In the finale, reverse all of it: stand still, light the locket, and let her look.

obstacles_and_puzzles.name: Every Bell Rings in His Room (the lure)
obstacles_and_puzzles.where: Harlan's bedroom bell pull → the parlor door downstairs
obstacles_and_puzzles.solution: Pull the embroidered bell pull by his bed. The parlor bell rings below, and Ada drops her patrol, investigation or search (never an active chase). She goes down the main stair and scratches at the locked parlor door for about 75 seconds, which clears the upper floor. The pull can be reused after a cooldown, and each time she comes back up you can hear her wet steps climbing.
obstacles_and_puzzles.clues: The bell you pulled at the front door rang off to the right, in the parlor (spatial audio). Bell wires and cranks run visibly along the cornices toward the parlor. Diary: 'Every pull in the house rings in the parlor now. She always comes to the bell.' The first use gives immediate feedback: the jangle, the drip receding down the stairs, and scratching heard through the floor grate.

obstacles_and_puzzles.name: Nailed Shut (pry in the thunder)
obstacles_and_puzzles.where: Ada's door, upper hallway beside the stair top
obstacles_and_puzzles.solution: Take the claw hammer from Harlan's windowsill. Pry the three boards one at a time, each inside a thunder roll: a lightning flash, about 1.5 s, then 2.5 s of rumble that masks all player noise. Prying outside the rumble is a 14 m noise that brings her back even from the parlor door. Hide in the armoire and carry on; pried boards stay pried. Assist: after two failures the storm flashes more often.
obstacles_and_puzzles.clues: Diary: 'Can't hear a thing under the thunder.' In B06 a thunderclap audibly swallows her own footsteps. The hammer sits beside a coffee can of the same square nails that seal his windows. The storm keeps a steady flash, count, rumble rhythm all night.

obstacles_and_puzzles.name: The Hem
obstacles_and_puzzles.solution: Read Ada's unsent letter, trapped under the sewing machine's presser foot. Pull the dust sheet off the dummy and cut the wedding dress's hem with the shears from her basket. The bundle holds the locket (key item), the 6:10 bus ticket and forty dollars. Then survive her visit in the wardrobe. A cold draft through its loose back boards stirs the dust sheets and shows the way to the servants' stair.
obstacles_and_puzzles.clues: The letter: 'the rest is sewn in the hem of my wedding dress... The ticket's there, and the locket. I can't wear his face anymore.' The snapshot in Harlan's room shows Ada at her machine beside the dress. Diary: 'Only picture left is in her locket, and that went down the well with her' explains why it matters and that Harlan believes it is gone. Diary: 'Nailed up her room. Can't go in there' explains why he never found it.

obstacles_and_puzzles.name: Let Her Look (the finale)
obstacles_and_puzzles.where: Entrance hall, between the foot of the stair and the parlor door
obstacles_and_puzzles.solution: With the locket open, raise it (right mouse) into the flashlight beam and stand still as she comes. When her hand lifts her head, she sees Harlan's face. She takes the locket and goes to him, the rope runs out, and the front door opens. Running is not an instant fail: she simply chases you, and the kitchen loop lets you try the approach again. After one death the scene restarts with the locket already raised.
obstacles_and_puzzles.clues: Diary: 'She can't find me if she can't see me... If she ever sees my face she'll know me.' The sack, the covered mirrors and the scratched photos all say his face is the weapon. The rule she has taught you all night (she sees only what is lit, and only with her head lifted) tells you how to show it. Harlan's bell-ringing turns frantic the moment you raise the locket.

designs.escape_theorem:
GOAL: leave alive through the front door and drive away.
1. The front door is the only exit. [Every sash is nailed, with the hammer and nail can on his sill; the kitchen door is bricked.]
2. The front door is worked from the parlor by a rope. [You saw it open and slam 'by itself'; the rope runs on pulleys along the hall cornice to a cleat in the parlor.]
3. The parlor is Harlan's, and you can fight neither him nor her. ⇒ The rope will move only if Harlan is removed, and only Ada can remove him.
4. Ada is not hunting you. She is hunting one face: his. [Diary: 'She can't find me if she can't see me'; the feed sack; crepe over every mirror; his face scratched out of every photo; she lifts her head to inspect every face she finds.]
5. If she sees his face, she will know him. [Diary: 'If she ever sees my face she'll know me, and that's the end of me.']
6. The only surviving image of his face is the locket. [Diary: 'Only picture left is in her locket, and that went down the well with her'. He is wrong.] Ada sewed it into the hem of her wedding dress. [Ada's letter.]
7. The dress is in Ada's room ⇐ the door is nailed ⇐ pry it with his hammer ⇐ without being heard, under the thunder [diary] ⇐ while a bell has sent her downstairs [diary: 'She always comes to the bell'].
8. She sees only what is lit, and only while her head is lifted. [Taught by every encounter.] ⇒ The locket must be in your beam, and you must let her come close enough to look.
THEREFORE: locket + light + stillness ⇒ she knows him ⇒ she takes Harlan ⇒ the rope runs out ⇒ the door opens. Fuel (a full can in the kitchen) ⇒ the car ⇒ the road.
COROLLARY (the sting): whoever holds the rope keeps the house, and she learns. [Diary: 'She works the latches now.']
items: Flashlight: steel two-cell, always equipped (F toggles). The beam lights your way, lures her when it touches her and makes you visible when she looks. In the finale it must light the locket.
Car keys: carried from the opening; used at dawn.
Claw hammer: from Harlan's windowsill; carried; pries the three boards on Ada's door.
Sewing shears: from Ada's basket; used in place to cut the hem (not carried).
Ada's locket: key item from the hem. Engraved 'A. from H. 1968', with a small water-stained photo of young Harlan inside. Right mouse raises it, open, into the beam.
Bus ticket (6:10, 12 Oct 1976) and forty dollars: found with the locket; lore only.
Full jerry can: from the kitchen; a dead traveler's siphoned gasoline, poured into your car at dawn. The empty can chalked RVX-318 stays behind.

Document, Harlan's diary p1: 'Oct 14 '76. She came up again. Did what Mother's book says: took the head and gave it back to the water. Holds her one night. God forgive me. Nailed up her room. Can't go in there.'

Document, Harlan's diary p2: 'She can't find me if she can't see me. Covered the glass. Cut myself out of the pictures. Wear the sack even to sleep. If she ever sees my face she'll know me, and that's the end of me. Only picture left is in her locket, and that went down the well with her.'

Document, Harlan's diary p3: 'Every pull in the house rings in the parlor now. She always comes to the bell. Can't hear a thing under the thunder. / The drifter kept her quiet near a month. Tried the Pruitt boy myself; didn't hold her an hour. She has to take them herself. / Filled the sign lamp from the Dodge. / She works the latches now. She learns.'

Document, Ada's unsent letter: 'Ruthie, Tuesday, the 6:10 to Carvel. He found the tin, so the rest is sewn in the hem of my wedding dress, the one thing in this house he'll never touch. The ticket's there, and the locket. I can't wear his face anymore, but I won't leave it for him. He says he'll put me down the well before he lets me go. Let him try. I'll be at the depot by six if I have to wa'

Document, the guest book: headed GUESTS, with columns Date / Name / Vehicle. Eleven lines from 1977 to 1994, each ruled through ('Nov 3 '77, drifter, on foot'; 'Jun 22 '79, D. Pruitt, '72 Dodge Dart'...). The last line has tonight's date, with name and vehicle blank.
Document, the October 1976 calendar: Tuesday 12 circled in pencil, '6:10'.

Documents, three photographs with Harlan's face knifed out: the wedding portrait (hall), 'Stroud's Gas & Feed, 1970' with the couple at the pump (landing), and Ada at her sewing machine beside the dress (Harlan's room).
designs.fail_and_checkpoints: Death is never gory and never long. It is a 3-second cutaway: her wet hand over the lens, her head lifted so close that the one eye fills the frame, then black and a bubbling rush of water (you are being taken to the cistern). The game then reloads instantly. Progress is never lost, only position: items, pried boards, opened doors and read documents all persist. Checkpoints: CP1 on the porch after the opening; CP2 in the hall as she rises (the parlor scene restarts in 3 s rather than replaying); CP3 at the armoire after the first hide; CP4 in Harlan's bedroom on taking the diary or hammer; CP5 after each pried board; CP6 in Ada's room on taking the locket; CP7 in the kitchen at the foot of the back stair; CP8 in the hall at the finale. The first hide cannot be failed: if you don't hold your breath, she lingers longer and then leaves. Adaptive assist: after 2 deaths in one section she moves 15% slower and her LOOK wind-up stretches from 1.2 to 1.6 s. After 3, the house helps: a shutter bangs at the far end of the floor and draws her off, or the storm sends thunder on cue. Finale safety: running is not an instant fail, because she just chases and the kitchen loop lets you approach again. After one finale death the scene restarts with the locket already raised; after two, she stops and waits for it. Soft hints (M3): if the player is stuck for 90 s, lightning picks out the next interactable. Every cutscene can be skipped after it has been seen once.

ending.name: The Keeping
ending.description: The only ending, earned by working through the escape theorem. Ada sees Harlan's face in your light, takes the locket and walks into the parlor, and in shadow she ends the man who has ended her every night for eighteen years. The rope runs out and the front door opens by itself: the man opened it to bring you in, and she opens it to let you go. Dawn, birdsong, and mist over the field of dead cars. A dead traveler's gasoline goes into your tank, the engine catches, the GAS sign's lantern gutters out as you pass, and the house sinks into the mirror. It is a real release after thirteen minutes of dread. Then the sting reframes it: you freed her from her keeper, not from the house.
ending.final_sting: Weeks later. In the rain, a different dashboard, a pickup with its fuel light blinking, rolls to a stop under the GAS sign. The lantern is lit again. Seen through the new traveler's eyes: a knock; the bell rings off to the right; the front door opens by itself. The guest book lies open. Its newest line reads HARLAN in wet, clumsy capitals, ruled through, with tonight's date and a blank beneath it. Through the first door on the right, from exactly the threshold and lens of the opening: candlelight, the tally wall, and Ada in his rocking chair with a round, heavy feed sack tied at the neck in her lap. The rocking stops. She lifts her own head in one hand, and with the other she raises the sack by its knot and turns its eyeholes to the doorway, just as he once turned hers. Both of them look at you. Smash to black. One bell. THE KEEPING.
